name: Terena
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Martins, Cosme Romero. 2009. Fonologia da língua Terena. Dissertação de Mestrado (Filologia e Língua Portuguesa), Faculdade de Filosofia, Letras e Ciências Humanas, Universidade de São Paulo. 85 pp. DOI 10.11606/d.8.2009.tde-04122009-162223; open copy at etnolinguistica.org (tese:martins-2009).
catalog_quote: [p. 59] O acento em Terena pode manifestar-se em uma das três primeiras sílabas. Limitação essa, denominada de “Restrição da Janela de Três Sílabas”, segundo a qual, o acento alcança maximamente a terceira sílaba a contar da borda esquerda da palavra (Kager, 1993). [...] [p. 62] Os dados dos padrões acentuais acima nos informa que o acento da língua é não previsível. Hipotetizamos que o acento da língua é livre, ou seja, já previamente definido no léxico. Por outro lado, o sistema acentual da língua sinaliza estar também governado por fatores morfológicos. Por exemplo, os diferentes padrões acentuais (2/3 – 1/3 – 1/2) parecem interagir com as diferentes classes de raízes (verbal ou nominal). Além do mais o acento demonstra ser cíclico. Ele se manifesta na raiz (1a posição) e depois se desloca em direção à borda direita da palavra (2a posição) quando são acrescidos sufixos tais como –ti e –na. [...] Podemos classificar a língua Terena como uma língua que constrói pés binários de cabeça à esquerda e insensível ao peso silábico (troqueu silábico). [...] [pp. 70-71] Partindo da hipótese de que o acento em Terena é livre, ou seja, a posição do acento primário já vem marcada na forma subjacente, podemos construir a grade métrica da palavra de cima para baixo (topdown).
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Language not in the catalog. Both Glottolog stress-title items are by Bendor-Samuel and neither could be opened: 'Stress in Terena' (TPS 61, 1962/63, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-968x.1962.tb00995.x) is Wiley-paywalled behind an automated-access block with no repository copy (Crossref/OpenAlex records saved), and 'Some prosodic features in Terena' (In Memory of J. R. Firth, 1966, pp. 30-39) exists only as an unavailable archive.org lending item. Its content is recoverable second-hand: Silva 2009 (cap. V) translates Bendor-Samuel's core claim that non-particle words are stressed on one of two syllables within the first three, the choice being grammatical, not phonological; Martins 2009 (p. 59, p. 62) gives the best first-hand statement read here (three-syllable left-edge window, lexically free but morphologically shifted two-position stress, acute vs circumflex accent types), and Ferreira 2021 (pp. 17-22) confirms morphologically conditioned shift from speaker checks. Priority: high for acquiring Bendor-Samuel 1962 (the primary description); medium for 1966 (possibly Firthian prosodies rather than word stress).

Limitação essa, denominada de “Restrição da Janela de Três Sílabas”, segundo a qual, o acento alcança maximamente a terceira sílaba a contar da borda esquerda da palavra (Kager, 1993). [...] [p. 62] Os dados dos padrões acentuais acima nos informa que o acento da língua é não previsível. Hipotetizamos que o acento da língua é livre, ou seja, já previamente definido no léxico. Por outro lado, o sistema acentual da língua sinaliza estar também governado por fatores morfológicos. [...] Além do mais o acento demonstra ser cíclico. Ele se manifesta na raiz (1a posição) e depois se desloca em direção à borda direita da palavra (2a posição) quando são acrescidos sufixos tais como –ti e –na.
new_statements.translation: [p. 59] Stress in Terena may appear on any one of the first three syllables. This limitation, called the 'Three-Syllable Window Restriction', means stress reaches at most the third syllable counting from the left edge of the word (Kager 1993). [...] [p. 62] The data on the stress patterns above tell us that the stress of the language is not predictable. We hypothesise that stress is free, i.e. already specified in the lexicon. On the other hand, the stress system also appears to be governed by morphological factors. [...] Moreover stress proves to be cyclic: it appears on the root (1st position) and then shifts toward the right edge of the word (2nd position) when suffixes such as -ti and -na are added.
new_statements.citation: Martins, Cosme Romero. 2009. Fonologia da língua Terena. Dissertação de Mestrado (Filologia e Língua Portuguesa), Universidade de São Paulo. 85 pp.

Hipotetizamos que o acento da língua é livre, ou seja, já previamente definido no léxico. Por outro lado, o sistema acentual da língua sinal…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (accent) falls on one of the first three syllables of the word; which of them is not phonologically predictable but lexically specified per root class and manipulated by morphology: each noun/verb has a '1st position' (root form, e.g. with definite possessor / one TAM value) and a '2nd position' one syllable to the right (with suffixes -ti 'unspecified possessor', -na, etc.), giving patterns 2~3, 1~3, 1~2. The accent comes in two phonetic types: acento I (acute: level pitch, gemination of the following consonant) and acento II (circumflex: falling pitch, lengthened vowel), themselves grammatically contrastive (íti 'blood' vs îti 'you'; pího 'when he went' vs pîho 'he went'). The final syllable is normally unstressed (extrametrical); a handful of nouns (with final glottal stop) and some verb forms carry word-final accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Martins builds weight-insensitive left-headed binary feet (syllabic trochees) bidirectionally outward from the lexically placed primary, degenerate feet banned, final stray syllable extrametrical (abstract p. 7; §4.6.5 pp. 69-71); Silva 2009 p. 90 notes most words have a primary and a secondary stress. No independent acoustic verification of secondaries.
new_statements.exceptions: Particles are outside the system (Bendor-Samuel apud Silva 2009 p. 87); a few nouns and di-/trisyllabic verbs have final stress (§4.6.6 pp. 71-72); Portuguese loans often keep their accent and do not shift under suffixation (Ferreira 2021 p. 22); prefix ko- 'causative' attracts the accent leftward (Ferreira 2021).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (morphological) word in citation/elicited forms; Martins §4.6.6-4.7 and Carvalho 2017 (apud Ferreira 2021 p. 21) note phrase-level and intonational melodies can alter the basic word profile (e.g. verb+object, noun+possessor take acento II on the 2nd syllable at phonological-phrase level). Whether the prominence is 'stress', 'tone' or 'pitch accent' is disputed: Aikhenvald 1999/2001 and Souza 2008 (Kinikinau) suspect tone; Butler 1977 speaks of two tones on one of the first three syllables; Carvalho 2021 calls it a 'tonal accent'; Martins 2009, Silva 2009, Butler 2001 treat it as accentual.
new_statements.identity_note: Martins 2009 and Silva 2009 describe Terena proper as spoken at Aldeia Cachoeirinha (Miranda, MS). Souza 2008 describes the Kinikinau variety (Aldeia São João, Bodoquena; Glottolog dialect kini1234 under tere1279) and explicitly does not mark accent, suspecting tone. Carvalho 2016 argues Terena, Chané, Guaná and Kinikinau are one language.

new_statements.quote: [p. 12, §2.2 'Acentos'] Na língua terena é sempre necessário marcar a sílaba acentuada porque não é predizível. É obrigatório decorar a acentuação de cada palavra. Dadas certas circunstâncias, o acento cai na última sílaba da palavra, mas normalmente fica numa das primeiras três sílabas. [...] Além destas situações pouco frequentes, cai o acento regularmente numa das primeiras 3 sílabas. [...] [p. 46, §13.2] Embora não haja regras que determinem a colocação do acento em substantivos, é útil notar que ele nunca ocorre após a terceira sílaba nem na sílaba final.
new_statements.translation: [p. 12] In the Terena language it is always necessary to mark the accented syllable because it is not predictable. One must memorise the accentuation of each word. Under certain circumstances the accent falls on the last syllable of the word, but normally it lies on one of the first three syllables. [...] Apart from these infrequent situations, the accent regularly falls on one of the first 3 syllables. [...] [p. 46] Although there are no rules that determine the placement of the accent in nouns, it is useful to note that it never occurs after the third syllable nor on the final syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's lexical coding from Martins 2009 on both points (accent 'não é predizível', must be memorised word by word; normally within the first three syllables, never after the third) and adds detail the record lacks: (a) marginal oxytone forms with final glottal stop (vocatives kalivonó', auxiliary phrases koyuhohí' kôe, hhingá'); (b) nouns never take final accent, so shortened 2-3-syllable forms shift the accent leftward as a circumflex ('acento deslocado': kurikéke ~ kurîke, hhevéhiko ~ hhêve); (c) two accent types (agudo: following consonant lengthened, level pitch; circunflexo: vowel lengthened, falling pitch) that alone distinguish pairs (íti 'sangue' / îti 'você'); (d…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is lexical: its syllable cannot be predicted and must be learnt per word; it normally falls on one of the first three syllables (never later than the third; nouns never on the final syllable), with a handful of oxytone forms ending in glottal stop (vocatives, some auxiliary phrases, hhingá'). Every noun and verb has two grammatically selected accent positions (1ª posição on syllable 1 or 2, 2ª posição one syllable further right, e.g. with -ti), giving lexical verb classes 1-2, 1-3, 2-3; two phonetic accent types (acute: level pitch, following consonant lengthened; circumflex: falling pitch, vowel lengthened) can be the only difference between words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. The work instead describes 'unidades de acentuação' (§2.4, §3.5): groups of two or more words carrying a single tonic accent, in which the first word loses its accent (xe'exa tapî'i, nikoti tapî'i), plus accentless function words (ra, ne, ako, avo, na, kuti, prepositions, kali/sêno/pô'i).
new_statements.exceptions: Oxytone forms with final glottal stop (vocative kalivonó'; auxiliary phrases koyuhohí' kôe; hhingá' 'vamos'); when the 3rd and 4th vowels form an accented group the accent goes to the 4th unless the word ends there (porexoâti vs ene porexôa); 'acento deslocado': accent retracts one syllable and becomes circumflex when suffix loss would leave it word-final in a 2-3-syllable noun (kurikéke > kurîke, tapi'íhiko > tapî'i, hhevéhiko > hhêve, takíkuke > tâki) and in short verbs (pihópo > pîho; pihopóne > pího), and may return to its normal syllable before yaa in fast speech (§13.1); some circumflexes are basic, not shifted (peîxou, tiûketi vs tiúketi).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Terena proper (SIL fieldwork, Mato Grosso do Sul villages), not the Kinikinau or Guaná/Chané varieties.

new_statements.quote: Há dois tipos de silabas acentuadas, simbolizadas por /^/ circunflexo e /´/ agudo. O acento agudo indica que uma sílaba é pronunciada com mais força e tom mais alto que as outras sílabas, e que a consoante seguinte é prolongada. O acento circunflexo indica que a sílaba é pronunciada com mais força que outras sílabas e com tom cadente, prolongando-se a vogal. Todo verbo apresenta duas posições fundamentais de intensidade, chamadas 'primeira' e 'segunda' posição. Existem três padrões de intensidade, e segundo um ou outro deles os verbos podem ser classificados de verbo 1-2, verbo 2-3 ou verbo 1-3.
new_statements.translation: There are two types of stressed syllables, symbolized by /^/ circumflex and /´/ acute. The acute accent indicates that a syllable is pronounced with more force and higher pitch than the other syllables, and that the following consonant is lengthened. The circumflex accent indicates that the syllable is pronounced with more force than other syllables and with falling pitch, the vowel being lengthened. Every verb has two basic stress positions, called 'first' and 'second' position. There are three stress patterns, and according to one or the other of them verbs can be classified as 1-2 verbs, 2-3 verbs or 1-3 verbs.
new_statements.citation: Daniel, Mary L. and Butler, Nancy E. (1978). Modo, extensão temporal, tempo verbal e relevância contrastiva na língua terêna. Brasília: Summer Institute of Linguistics. iii+71 pp.

Butler 1978/2007 states the same system from the primary SIL fieldwork and adds detail: the explicit verb classes 1-2 / 2-3 / 1-3, the phonetic definition of the two accents (force + high vs falling pitch, C- vs V-lengthening), the ban on final-syllable acute accent, the acute->circumflex alternation under one-syllable shift, and the grammatical triggers of second position (-ti, temporal/sequential clauses, subjective emphasis, conditionals vs im…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (called acento / intensidade) is lexically classed and grammatically deployed: every verb has two stress positions within the first three syllables. 'First position' (the basic stress of actual-mood verbs, also objective/locative emphasis, imperatives) falls on syllable 1 or 2 depending on the verb; 'second position' (subjective emphasis, temporal/sequential clauses, conditionals, obligatory with durative -ti and after conjunctions like imókone) falls one or two syllables further right, giving verb classes 1-2 (íhikaxovo / ihíkaxovo), 2-3 (oyé'eko / oye'éko) and 1-3 (ókonukoa / okonúkoa). Two phonetic accent types: acute = greater force + higher pitch + lengthened following consonant; circumflex = greater force + falling pitch + lengthened vowel. Pitch is described as a correlate of the accent, not as lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Nota 22 (p. 28): acute accent is not permitted on a word-final syllable; with the short verb 'chegar' the vowel of suffix -ne is reduplicated so the accent does not land on the final syllable. Nota 1 (p. 27): word length can cause accent displacement, especially in short verbs; a basic acute accent shifted one syllable rightward becomes circumflex, shifted two syllables it stays acute. Apêndice 2: second-position stress is obligatory with durative -ti and after certain conjunctions (imókone 'até'); mood choice is independent of stress position.
new_statements.identity_note: Terena proper (Butler and Ekdahl SIL fieldwork from 1966, 'região sudoeste do Estado de Mato Grosso', i.e. present Mato Grosso do Sul); the copy read is the 2007 revision 'com ortografia atualizada' of the 1978 Portuguese translation (by Mary L. Daniel) of Butler's study, 38 pp. rather than the iii+71 pp. of the 1978 print.

sources.note: Reviews Bendor-Samuel 1960-62, Ekdahl & Butler 1979 (p.12: circumflex = reinforced syllable with lengthened vowel and falling tone; acute = reinforced syllable with lengthening of following sound; accent distinctive and tied to grammatical function), Martins 2009 (three-syllable window, lexical), Silva 2009, Aikhenvald 1999/2001 (tonal hypothesis); argues accent shift is morphophonologically conditioned: shifts rightward with suffixes -ti, -mo, -na, -xo (hhêve -> hhevêti, káxe -> kaxéna), toward prefix with causative ko-; loans often do not shift; not conclusive on stress vs tone vs pitch acc…

sources.note: Cap. sources.quote: [Silva 2009, paraphrasing Bendor-Samuel 'Stress in Terena', fn. 20] "De acordo com Bendor-Samuel (1963b), há um contraste na colocação do acento em palavras (exceto partículas) que são acentuadas em uma das duas, exceto as primeiras três sílabas da palavra. A seleção da primeira ou segunda dessas duas sílabas acentuadas tem funções gramaticais importantes; algumas vezes, por exemplo, o acento distingue o sujeito do objeto. [...] Essa seleção entre as duas sílabas acentuais não é previsível com nenhuma base fonológica [...] unicamente determinada por fatores gramaticais" (EN: according to B-S, words other than particles are stressed on one of two of the first three syllables; choice between the two is grammatically, not phonologically, determined).
sources.locator: Full text not opened. Content known only through Silva 2009, cap. V 'O acento' (pp. 86-87, fn. 20 'Tradução nossa'), Martins 2009 §4.2 p. 59, Ferreira 2021 pp. 15-17.
sources.note: Per the secondary reports (not the article itself): every Terena word except particles has stress on one of two syllables lying within the first three syllables of the word; which of the two positions is used is not phonologically predictable but is set by morphology/syntax (e.g. it can distinguish subject from object); where that positional contrast is neutralised, a contrast between two sets of phonetic exponents of stress (the acute vs circumflex 'accent I/II') carries the grammatical contrast. Martins 2009 p. 59 cites the same paper for 'one of the first three syllables' and for Terena be…
